pupilNote: Sophia, girl aged 6, home educated, Year 2 from September 2026. There is NO daily time target. Every session is designed to be 10-20 minutes, game-like, heavy on speaking, listening and doing. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1 - she is expected to read whole books that match her phonics, write a piece over several days, and hold a spelling rule in her head - but she is still six, so instructions are spoken rather than read, thinking happens out loud, and objects stay in her hands. Stop when she has had enough; there is no penalty for doing less on any given day.

sessionDesign.readingLoadForChild: light but growing - she reads books matched to her phonics and reads her own writing aloud, but task instructions are still spoken, not read

phonicsProgramme.name: Little Wandle Letters and Sounds Revised (2021) and Little Wandle Spelling (Year 2)
phonicsProgramme.status: DfE-validated systematic synthetic phonics programme, continued from the Year 1 scheme
phonicsProgramme.yearGroupPhase: Year 2 is consolidation, not new GPCs. Autumn 1 is the published Phase 5 review block; Autumn 2 is 'Bridge to spelling'; Spring and Summer are Little Wandle Spelling Units 1-14, which give full coverage of the statutory English Appendix 1 Year 2 spelling requirements.
phonicsProgramme.warning: The order in which Little Wandle teaches its Phase 5 review graphemes and its spelling units must not be changed. It is reproduced here as published; only the pace has been adjusted to fit the 39-week England year.

phonicsScreeningCheck.status: The phonics screening check remains STATUTORY. It is the only statutory assessment in Key Stage 1. Any child who did not meet the expected standard in Year 1 must be considered for a re-take in Year 2.
phonicsScreeningCheck.when: The DfE has published the 2027 window: the check must be administered within the one-week period beginning Monday 14 June 2027. In this scheme that is Summer 2, week 2 (week 34 of 39).
phonicsScreeningCheck.format: 40 words in two sections of 20, read one-to-one aloud, untimed. Section 1: 12 pseudo-words then 8 real words. Section 2: 8 pseudo-words then 12 real words.
phonicsScreeningCheck.pseudoWords: 20 of the 40 words are pseudo-words. Each is shown beside a picture of an imaginary creature so the child knows it is not a real word and must decode it.
phonicsScreeningCheck.section1Content: Simple structures (CVC, VCC, CCVC, CVCC) using single letters, the consonant digraphs ch, ck, ff, ll, ng, sh, ss, th, zz, and the vowel digraphs ar, ee, oi, oo, or.
phonicsScreeningCheck.section2Content: More complex structures, plus ph, wh, a-e, ai, au, aw, ay, ea, e-e, er, ew, i-e, ie, ir, oa, o-e, ou, ow, oy, ue, u-e, ur, air, igh and alternative pronunciations.
phonicsScreeningCheck.threshold: The expected standard has been 32 out of 40 in recent years. The DfE confirms and publishes the threshold mark each June, after the check window closes.
phonicsScreeningCheck.howToHandleItAtHome: Run it as a game, one-to-one, untimed, never scored aloud in front of her. Week 33 is deliberately light preparation and week 34 protects her relationship with reading. Anxiety costs more marks than gaps in phonic knowledge do.

endOfKeyStage1Assessment.headline: End of Key Stage 1 assessment is NOT statutory. It has been non-statutory since the 2023/24 academic year and remains so for 2026/27.
endOfKeyStage1Assessment.whatDfESays: On 20 July 2022 the DfE announced that end of key stage 1 (KS1) assessments would become non-statutory from the academic year 2023 to 2024 onwards. The gov.uk collection states: 'Teacher assessment at the end of KS1 (key stage 1) is optional, including any related moderation and reporting activities.' The optional guidance states: 'There is now no statutory requirement to carry out end of KS1 teacher assessment.'
endOfKeyStage1Assessment.ks1Sats: The end of Key Stage 1 national curriculum tests, commonly called KS1 SATs, are therefore optional. They are not a test this child needs to sit, and no test paper is planned for in this scheme.
endOfKeyStage1Assessment.whatIsStillStatutory: The phonics screening check in Key Stage 1 remains statutory, including the Year 2 re-take. That is the only statutory Key Stage 1 assessment.
endOfKeyStage1Assessment.targetUsedInThisScheme: The non-statutory 'Teacher assessment frameworks at the end of key stage 1' (Standards and Testing Agency, published 29 April 2024) is used here as the target rather than any test. Its 'working at the expected standard' descriptors for reading, writing, mathematics and science are reproduced below and every one of them is deliberately carried by named lessons in this scheme.
expectedStandardReading: accurately read most words of 2 or more syllables
read most words containing common suffixes

in age-appropriate books, read most words accurately without overt sounding and blending, and with sufficient fluency to allow them to focus on their understanding rather than on decoding individual words
in age-appropriate books, sound out most unfamiliar words accurately, without undue hesitation
in a book that they can already read fluently, check it makes sense to them, correcting any inaccurate reading
in a book that they can already read fluently, answer questions and make some inferences
in a book that they can already read fluently, explain what has happened so far in what they have read
expectedStandardWriting: write simple, coherent narratives about personal experiences and those of others (real or fictional)
write about real events, recording these simply and clearly
demarcate most sentences in their writing with capital letters and full stops, and use question marks correctly when required
use present and past tense mostly correctly and consistently
use co-ordination (such as or/and/but) and some subordination (such as when/if/that/because) to join clauses
segment spoken words into phonemes and represent these by graphemes, spelling many of these words correctly and making phonically plausible attempts at others
form capital letters and digits of the correct size, orientation and relationship to one another and to lower-case letters
use spacing between words that reflects the size of the letters
expectedStandardMathematics: read scales in divisions of ones, twos, fives and tens
partition any two-digit number into different combinations of tens and ones, explaining their thinking verbally, in pictures or using apparatus
add and subtract any 2 two-digit numbers using an efficient strategy, explaining their method verbally, in pictures or using apparatus
recall all number bonds to and within 10 and use these to reason with and calculate bonds to and within 20, recognising other associated additive relationships
recall multiplication and division facts for 2, 5 and 10 and use them to solve simple problems, demonstrating an understanding of commutativity as necessary
identify 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/4, 3/4 of a number or shape, and know that all parts must be equal parts of the whole
use different coins to make the same amount
read the time on a clock to the nearest 15 minutes
name and describe properties of 2D and 3D shapes, including number of sides, vertices, edges, faces and lines of symmetry
expectedStandardScience: ask their own questions about what they notice

use different types of scientific enquiry to gather and record data, using simple equipment where appropriate, to answer questions (observing changes over time; noticing patterns; grouping and classifying things; carrying out simple comparative tests; finding things out using secondary sources of information)
communicate their ideas, what they do and what they find out in a variety of ways
describe the importance of exercise, a balanced diet and hygiene for humans
describe the basic needs of animals for survival and the main changes as young animals, including humans, grow into adults
describe the basic needs of plants for survival and the impact of changing these and the main changes as seeds and bulbs grow into mature plants
identify whether things are alive, dead or have never lived
describe how animals get their food from other animals and/or from plants, and use simple food chains to describe these relationships
name different plants and animals and describe how they are suited to different habitats
compare the suitability of everyday materials for different uses

readyToProgressYear2.2NPV-2: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2NPV-2): reason about the location of any two-digit number in the linear number system, including identifying the previous and next multiple of 10
readyToProgressYear2.2NF-1: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2NF-1): secure fluency in addition and subtraction facts within 10, through continued practice
readyToProgressYear2.2AS-1: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2AS-1): add and subtract across 10
readyToProgressYear2.2AS-2: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2AS-2): recognise the subtraction structure of 'difference' and answer questions of the form 'How many more...?'
readyToProgressYear2.2AS-3: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2AS-3): add and subtract within 100 by applying related one-digit addition and subtraction facts: add and subtract only ones or only tens to/from a two-digit number
readyToProgressYear2.2AS-4: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2AS-4): add and subtract within 100 by applying related one-digit addition and subtraction facts: add and subtract any 2 two-digit numbers

verifiedAgainstPrimarySources: The statutory Year 2 programmes of study for English, Mathematics and Science were read from the gov.uk national curriculum pages (DfE, 2013). Every ncRef in this file quotes that wording.

English Appendix 1 (Spelling) was read from the gov.uk PDF (English_Appendix_1_-_Spelling.pdf). Every Year 2 statutory spelling row is reproduced with its rule wording and its example words: ge/dge, g before e i y, c before e i y, kn/gn, wr, -le, -el, -al, -il, -y for /igh/, -es after y, y-to-i before -ed/-er/-est, drop-the-e, doubling, a before l and ll, o for /u/, -ey for /ee/, a after w and qu, or after w, ar after w, s for /zh/, the suffixes -ment/-ness/-ful/-less/-ly, contractions, the possessive apostrophe (singular), -tion, homophones, and the common exception words.

The Year 2 common exception word list is reproduced verbatim and in printed order. It contains 64 words. The Appendix 1 note that 'great, break and steak are the only common words where the /ai/ sound is spelt ea' is taught explicitly in week 9.

English Appendix 2 (Vocabulary, grammar and punctuation) was read from the gov.uk PDF. The full Year 2 row is quoted: Word (nouns with -ness and -er and by compounding; adjectives with -ful and -less; -er and -est in adjectives and -ly to turn adjectives into adverbs); Sentence (subordination with when/if/that/because and co-ordination with or/and/but; expanded noun phrases; how grammatical patterns indicate statement, question, exclamation or command); Text (consistent present and past tense; the progressive form); Punctuation (capital letters, full stops, question marks and exclamation marks; commas in lists; apostrophes for omission and singular possession); and the fourteen Year 2 terminology items.

The Year 2 statutory maths programme of study was read in full from gov.uk and every strand is covered: number and place value, addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, fractions, measurement, geometry (properties of shapes; position and direction), and statistics.

The DfE ready-to-progress criteria for Year 2 were read verbatim from Maths guidance: year 2 (DfE, 2020). All ten - 2NPV-1, 2NPV-2, 2NF-1, 2AS-1, 2AS-2, 2AS-3, 2AS-4, 2MD-1, 2MD-2 and 2G-1 - are quoted in full and each is mapped onto named weeks.

The Year 2 statutory science programme of study was read from gov.uk: Living things and their habitats (4 bullets), Plants (2 bullets), Animals including humans (3 bullets) and Uses of everyday materials (2 bullets), plus the six Key Stage 1 working scientifically bullets.

PHONICS SCREENING CHECK 2027: the exact date was verified on the gov.uk guidance page 'Primary assessments: future dates'. For academic year 2026 to 2027 the check must be administered within the one-week period beginning MONDAY 14 JUNE 2027. In this scheme's 39-week shape that falls in Summer 2, week 2. The Year 1 scheme flagged this date as unverified; it is now confirmed.

PHONICS SCREENING CHECK RE-TAKE: the phonics screening check assessment and reporting arrangements on gov.uk confirm that pupils in Year 2 who have not taken the check before, or who did not meet the expected standard in the previous year's check, must also take the check, and that schools are expected to maintain a programme of support for those pupils. The check structure (40 words, 20 real and 20 pseudo-words, two sections, one-to-one, untimed) was verified on gov.uk. The threshold mark has been 32 out of 40 in recent years and is confirmed by the DfE each June.

END OF KEY STAGE 1 ASSESSMENT: verified on gov.uk. The non-statutory teacher assessment frameworks page states: 'On 20 July 2022, we announced that end of key stage 1 (KS1) assessments would become non-statutory from the academic year 2023 to 2024 onwards.' The gov.uk collection page states: 'Teacher assessment at the end of KS1 (key stage 1) is optional, including any related moderation and reporting activities.' The optional KS1 teacher assessment guidance states: 'There is now no statutory requirement to carry out end of KS1 teacher assessment' and 'The phonics screening check in KS1 remains statutory.' The 2025-26 guidance was last updated on 29 September 2025 and the non-statutory frameworks were published on 29 April 2024. All four 'working at the expected standard' descriptor sets (English reading, English writing, mathematics, science) were read from gov.uk and are reproduced verbatim in this file's endOfKeyStage1Assessment block.

Little Wandle Year 2 provision was checked against Little Wandle published documents: Little Wandle Spelling Year 2 is structured as Autumn 1 Phase 5 review (5 weeks), Autumn 2 Bridge to spelling (5 weeks), then Spelling Units 1-14 across Spring and Summer (20 weeks). Phase 5 review and Bridge to spelling lessons are published as 25-30 minute daily lessons and the Spelling units as 15-minute lessons four times a week; both are broken into shorter playful sessions here to suit an untimed home-education setting. The published Phase 5 review grapheme sets, the Bridge-to-spelling weekly focuses and the fourteen spelling unit titles are reproduced in the week 'unit' fields.

The White Rose Maths Year 2 block sequence was checked at block level: Autumn - place value, addition and subtraction (published as a five-week block), shape; Spring - money, multiplication and division (published as a five-week block), length and height, mass/capacity/temperature; Summer - fractions, time, statistics, position and direction.
notVerifiedOrProfessionalJudgement: The 2026/27 term dates and the 39-week shape. England has no single national school calendar; the dates given are a typical maintained-school pattern and should be adjusted to suit the family. The phonics screening check week (beginning Monday 14 June 2027) IS verified and falls in Summer 2 week 2 of this pattern; if the family's term dates differ, that week must be moved to match the real date, not the other way round.

Little Wandle publishes its Year 2 half terms as five teaching weeks each (30 weeks in total). The England year used here has 7, 7, 6, 5, 7 and 7 weeks. The published content has therefore been spread across the extra weeks. The ORDER is unchanged - no grapheme, unit or rule has been moved earlier or later relative to any other - only the pace is gentler, which suits an untimed home-education setting. The extra weeks in Summer 1 and Summer 2 carry the -tion unit, a homophone review, screening-check preparation and an extended writing project.

Little Wandle's published Year 2 progression lists 'prickly spellings' and homophones per unit; where those overlap the statutory Year 2 word list they are used, and the distribution of the 64 statutory common exception words across the 39 weeks is the compiler's, not Little Wandle's.

The distribution of White Rose Maths blocks into specific weeks is the compiler's, matched to the 39-week shape. White Rose publishes week counts for the two five-week blocks (addition and subtraction; multiplication and division) and those are honoured; the remaining allocations are professional judgement.
The mapping of individual ready-to-progress criteria onto individual weeks is the compiler's. The criteria wording itself is quoted verbatim from the DfE.

The placement of the four Year 2 science topics into half terms is the compiler's, chosen so that habitat fieldwork falls in warm weather and the plant-growing investigation has three weeks to run. The statutory content itself is complete and quoted.

The Discover themes (Mapmakers, Journeys Then and Now, A Contrasting Place: Kenya, Two Queens, Wild Places, Around the World and Home Again) are the compiler's. The Key Stage 1 history, geography, art and design and computing programmes of study are not split by year group, so the choice of content within them is a school-level decision. Kenya is chosen as the contrasting non-European locality; any other non-European locality would satisfy the statutory requirement equally.

Lesson titles, 'I can' objectives, key vocabulary, the misconceptions listed, the playful assessment activities and the knowledge components are written by the compiler from established Key Stage 1 practice. They are not quoted from any published scheme.

Historical facts used in Discover (the Wright brothers' first powered flight in 1903, the reigns of Elizabeth I 1558-1603 and Elizabeth II 1952-2022) are standard reference facts and were not re-verified against a primary archival source for this document.

The claim that the phonics screening check threshold has been 32 out of 40 'in recent years' reflects recent published thresholds; the DfE confirms the actual threshold each June and it should be checked rather than assumed.

ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.gedge: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /dj/ sound spelt as ge and dge at the end of words, and sometimes spelt as g elsewhere in words before e, i and y - the letter j is never used for the /dj/ sound at the end of English words; at the end of a word, the /dj/ sound is spelt -dge straight after the short vowel sounds, otherwise it is spelt as -ge (badge, edge, bridge, dodge, fudge, age, huge, change, charge, bulge, village)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.g_j: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /dj/ sound is often spelt as g before e, i, and y; the /dj/ sound is always spelt as j before a, o and u (gem, giant, magic, giraffe, energy, jacket, jar, jog, join, adjust)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.c_s: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /s/ sound spelt c before e, i and y (race, ice, cell, city, fancy)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.kngn: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /n/ sound spelt kn and (less often) gn at the beginning of words - the 'k' and 'g' at the beginning of these words was sounded hundreds of years ago (knock, know, knee, gnat, gnaw)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.wr: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /r/ sound spelt wr at the beginning of words - this spelling probably also reflects an old pronunciation (write, written, wrote, wrong, wrap)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.le: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /l/ or /ul/ sound spelt -le at the end of words - the -le spelling is the most common spelling for this sound at the end of words (table, apple, bottle, little, middle)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.el: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /l/ or /ul/ sound spelt -el at the end of words - the -el spelling is much less common than -le; -el is used after m, n, r, s, v, w and more often than not after s (camel, tunnel, squirrel, travel, towel, tinsel)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.al: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /l/ or /ul/ sound spelt -al at the end of words - not many nouns end in -al, but many adjectives do (metal, pedal, capital, hospital, animal)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.il: English Appendix 1 (Y2): words ending -il - there are not many of these words (pencil, fossil, nostril)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.y_igh: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /igh/ sound spelt -y at the end of words - this is by far the most common spelling for this sound at the end of words (cry, fly, dry, try, reply, July)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.esy: English Appendix 1 (Y2): adding -es to nouns and verbs ending in -y - the y is changed to i before -es is added (flies, tries, replies, copies, babies, carries)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.yi: English Appendix 1 (Y2): adding -ed, -ing, -er and -est to a root word ending in -y with a consonant before it - the y is changed to i before -ed, -er and -est are added, but not before -ing as this would result in ii (copied, copier, happier, happiest, cried, replied, copying, crying, replying)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.drope: English Appendix 1 (Y2): adding the endings -ing, -ed, -er, -est and -y to words ending in -e with a consonant before it - the -e at the end of the root word is dropped before -ing, -ed, -er, -est, -y or any other suffix beginning with a vowel letter is added; exception: being (hiking, hiked, hiker, nicer, nicest, shiny)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.double: English Appendix 1 (Y2): adding -ing, -ed, -er, -est and -y to words of one syllable ending in a single consonant letter after a single vowel letter - the last consonant letter of the root word is doubled to keep the short vowel sound; exception: the letter x is never doubled (patting, patted, humming, hummed, dropping, dropped, sadder, saddest, fatter, fattest, runner, runny)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.all: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /or/ sound spelt a before l and ll - the /or/ sound ('or') is usually spelt as a before l and ll (all, ball, call, walk, talk, always)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.o_u: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /u/ sound spelt o (other, mother, brother, nothing, Monday)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.ey: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /ee/ sound spelt -ey - the plural of these words is formed by the addition of -s (key, donkey, monkey, chimney, valley)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.wa: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /o/ sound spelt a after w and qu - a is the most common spelling for the /o/ ('hot') sound after w and qu (want, watch, wander, quantity, squash)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.wor: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /ur/ sound spelt or after w - there are not many of these words (word, work, worm, world, worth)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.war: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /or/ sound spelt ar after w - there are not many of these words (war, warm, towards)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.zh: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /zh/ sound spelt s (television, treasure, usual)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.suffixes: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the suffixes -ment, -ness, -ful, -less and -ly - if a suffix starts with a consonant letter, it is added straight on to most root words without any change to the last letter of those words (enjoyment, sadness, careful, playful, hopeless, plainness, badly); exceptions: argument; root words ending in -y with a consonant before it but only if the root word has more than one syllable (merriment, happiness, plentiful, penniless, happily)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.contract: English Appendix 1 (Y2): contractions - in contractions, the apostrophe shows where a letter or letters would be if the words were written in full (can't, didn't, hasn't, couldn't, it's, I'll); it's means it is or sometimes it has, but it's is never used for the possessive
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.poss: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the possessive apostrophe (singular nouns) - Megan's, Ravi's, the girl's, the child's, the man's
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.tion: English Appendix 1 (Y2): words ending in -tion (station, fiction, motion, national, section)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.homophones: English Appendix 1 (Y2): homophones and near-homophones - it is important to know the difference in meaning between homophones (there/their/they're, here/hear, quite/quiet, see/sea, bare/bear, one/won, sun/son, to/too/two, be/bee, blue/blew, night/knight)
ncReferenceIndex.E.A1.cew2: English Appendix 1 (Y2): common exception words - the Year 2 word list of 64 words in which the GPCs do not all fit what has been taught so far, together with the note that great, break and steak are the only common words where the /ai/ sound is spelt ea
ncReferenceIndex.E.A2.word: English Appendix 2 (Y2) Word: formation of nouns using suffixes such as -ness, -er and by compounding [for example, whiteboard, superman]; formation of adjectives using suffixes such as -ful, -less; use of the suffixes -er, -est in adjectives and the use of -ly in Standard English to turn adjectives into adverbs
ncReferenceIndex.E.A2.sentence: English Appendix 2 (Y2) Sentence: subordination (using when, if, that, because) and co-ordination (using or, and, but); expanded noun phrases for description and specification [for example, the blue butterfly, plain flour, the man in the moon]; how the grammatical patterns in a sentence indicate its function as a statement, question, exclamation or command
ncReferenceIndex.E.A2.text: English Appendix 2 (Y2) Text: correct choice and consistent use of present tense and past tense throughout writing; use of the progressive form of verbs in the present and past tense to mark actions in progress [for example, she is drumming, he was shouting]
ncReferenceIndex.E.A2.punct: English Appendix 2 (Y2) Punctuation: use of capital letters, full stops, question marks and exclamation marks to demarcate sentences; commas to separate items in a list; apostrophes to mark where letters are missing in spelling and to mark singular possession in nouns [for example, the girl's name]
ncReferenceIndex.E.A2.terms: English Appendix 2 (Y2) Terminology for pupils: noun, noun phrase, statement, question, exclamation, command, compound, suffix, adjective, adverb, verb, tense (past, present), apostrophe, comma
ncReferenceIndex.M.NPV1: Maths Y2 Number - number and place value: count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward
ncReferenceIndex.M.NPV2: Maths Y2 Number - number and place value: recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (10s, 1s)
ncReferenceIndex.M.NPV3: Maths Y2 Number - number and place value: identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line
ncReferenceIndex.M.NPV4: Maths Y2 Number - number and place value: compare and order numbers from 0 up to 100; use <, > and = signs
ncReferenceIndex.M.NPV5: Maths Y2 Number - number and place value: read and write numbers to at least 100 in numerals and in words
ncReferenceIndex.M.NPV6: Maths Y2 Number - number and place value: use place value and number facts to solve problems
ncReferenceIndex.M.AS1: Maths Y2 Number - addition and subtraction: solve problems with addition and subtraction using concrete objects and pictorial representations, including those involving numbers, quantities and measures, and applying their increasing knowledge of mental and written methods
ncReferenceIndex.M.AS2: Maths Y2 Number - addition and subtraction: recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100
ncReferenceIndex.M.AS3: Maths Y2 Number - addition and subtraction: add and subtract numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including: a two-digit number and 1s; a two-digit number and 10s; 2 two-digit numbers; adding 3 one-digit numbers
ncReferenceIndex.M.AS4: Maths Y2 Number - addition and subtraction: show that addition of 2 numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of 1 number from another cannot
ncReferenceIndex.M.AS5: Maths Y2 Number - addition and subtraction: recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction and use this to check calculations and solve missing number problems
ncReferenceIndex.M.MD1: Maths Y2 Number - multiplication and division: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, including recognising odd and even numbers
ncReferenceIndex.M.MD2: Maths Y2 Number - multiplication and division: calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division within the multiplication tables and write them using the multiplication (x), division (/) and equals (=) signs
ncReferenceIndex.M.MD3: Maths Y2 Number - multiplication and division: show that multiplication of 2 numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of 1 number by another cannot
ncReferenceIndex.M.MD4: Maths Y2 Number - multiplication and division: solve problems involving multiplication and division, using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and multiplication and division facts, including problems in contexts
ncReferenceIndex.M.F1: Maths Y2 Number - fractions: recognise, find, name and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4 and 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects or quantity
ncReferenceIndex.M.F2: Maths Y2 Number - fractions: write simple fractions, for example 1/2 of 6 = 3 and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
ncReferenceIndex.M.ME1: Maths Y2 Measurement: choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure length/height in any direction (m/cm); mass (kg/g); temperature (C); capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit, using rulers, scales, thermometers and measuring vessels
ncReferenceIndex.M.ME2: Maths Y2 Measurement: compare and order lengths, mass, volume/capacity and record the results using >, < and =
ncReferenceIndex.M.ME3: Maths Y2 Measurement: recognise and use symbols for pounds and pence; combine amounts to make a particular value
ncReferenceIndex.M.ME4: Maths Y2 Measurement: find different combinations of coins that equal the same amounts of money
ncReferenceIndex.M.ME5: Maths Y2 Measurement: solve simple problems in a practical context involving addition and subtraction of money of the same unit, including giving change
ncReferenceIndex.M.ME6: Maths Y2 Measurement: compare and sequence intervals of time
ncReferenceIndex.M.ME7: Maths Y2 Measurement: tell and write the time to five minutes, including quarter past/to the hour and draw the hands on a clock face to show these times
ncReferenceIndex.M.ME8: Maths Y2 Measurement: know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day
ncReferenceIndex.M.GP1: Maths Y2 Geometry - properties of shapes: identify and describe the properties of 2-D shapes, including the number of sides, and line symmetry in a vertical line
ncReferenceIndex.M.GP2: Maths Y2 Geometry - properties of shapes: identify and describe the properties of 3-D shapes, including the number of edges, vertices and faces
ncReferenceIndex.M.GP3: Maths Y2 Geometry - properties of shapes: identify 2-D shapes on the surface of 3-D shapes, [for example, a circle on a cylinder and a triangle on a pyramid]
ncReferenceIndex.M.GP4: Maths Y2 Geometry - properties of shapes: compare and sort common 2-D and 3-D shapes and everyday objects
ncReferenceIndex.M.GPD1: Maths Y2 Geometry - position and direction: order and arrange combinations of mathematical objects in patterns and sequences
ncReferenceIndex.M.GPD2: Maths Y2 Geometry - position and direction: use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction and movement, including movement in a straight line and distinguishing between rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise)
ncReferenceIndex.M.ST1: Maths Y2 Statistics: interpret and construct simple pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams and tables
ncReferenceIndex.M.ST2: Maths Y2 Statistics: ask and answer simple questions by counting the number of objects in each category and sorting the categories by quantity
ncReferenceIndex.M.ST3: Maths Y2 Statistics: ask and answer questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
ncReferenceIndex.S.WS1: Science KS1 Working scientifically: asking simple questions and recognising that they can be answered in different ways
ncReferenceIndex.S.WS2: Science KS1 Working scientifically: observing closely, using simple equipment
ncReferenceIndex.S.WS3: Science KS1 Working scientifically: performing simple tests
ncReferenceIndex.S.WS4: Science KS1 Working scientifically: identifying and classifying
ncReferenceIndex.S.WS5: Science KS1 Working scientifically: using their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions
ncReferenceIndex.S.WS6: Science KS1 Working scientifically: gathering and recording data to help in answering questions

ncReferenceIndex.S.LH2: Science Y2 Living things and their habitats: identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited and describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of different kinds of animals and plants, and how they depend on each other
ncReferenceIndex.S.LH3: Science Y2 Living things and their habitats: identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including microhabitats
ncReferenceIndex.S.LH4: Science Y2 Living things and their habitats: describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify and name different sources of food
ncReferenceIndex.S.PL1: Science Y2 Plants: observe and describe how seeds and bulbs grow into mature plants
ncReferenceIndex.S.PL2: Science Y2 Plants: find out and describe how plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy
ncReferenceIndex.S.AN1: Science Y2 Animals, including humans: notice that animals, including humans, have offspring which grow into adults
ncReferenceIndex.S.AN2: Science Y2 Animals, including humans: find out about and describe the basic needs of animals, including humans, for survival (water, food and air)
ncReferenceIndex.S.AN3: Science Y2 Animals, including humans: describe the importance for humans of exercise, eating the right amounts of different types of food, and hygiene
ncReferenceIndex.S.UM1: Science Y2 Uses of everyday materials: identify and compare the suitability of a variety of everyday materials, including wood, metal, plastic, glass, brick, rock, paper and cardboard for particular uses
ncReferenceIndex.S.UM2: Science Y2 Uses of everyday materials: find out how the shapes of solid objects made from some materials can be changed by squashing, bending, twisting and stretching
ncReferenceIndex.H.KS1: History KS1: pupils should develop an awareness of the past, using common words and phrases relating to the passing of time; know where the people and events they study fit within a chronological framework and identify similarities and differences between ways of life in different periods; use a wide vocabulary of everyday historical terms
ncReferenceIndex.H.1: History KS1: changes within living memory - where appropriate, these should be used to reveal aspects of change in national life
ncReferenceIndex.H.2: History KS1: events beyond living memory that are significant nationally or globally [for example, the Great Fire of London, the first aeroplane flight or events commemorated through festivals or anniversaries]
ncReferenceIndex.H.3: History KS1: the lives of significant individuals in the past who have contributed to national and international achievements; some should be used to compare aspects of life in different periods
ncReferenceIndex.H.4: History KS1: significant historical events, people and places in their own locality
ncReferenceIndex.G.L1: Geography KS1 Locational knowledge: name and locate the world's seven continents and five oceans
ncReferenceIndex.G.L2: Geography KS1 Locational knowledge: name, locate and identify characteristics of the four countries and capital cities of the United Kingdom and its surrounding seas
ncReferenceIndex.G.P1: Geography KS1 Place knowledge: understand geographical similarities and differences through studying the human and physical geography of a small area of the United Kingdom, and of a small area in a contrasting non-European country
ncReferenceIndex.G.HP1: Geography KS1 Human and physical geography: identify seasonal and daily weather patterns in the United Kingdom and the location of hot and cold areas of the world in relation to the Equator and the North and South Poles
ncReferenceIndex.G.HP2: Geography KS1 Human and physical geography: use basic geographical vocabulary to refer to key physical features, including: beach, cliff, coast, forest, hill, mountain, sea, ocean, river, soil, valley, vegetation, season and weather
ncReferenceIndex.G.HP3: Geography KS1 Human and physical geography: use basic geographical vocabulary to refer to key human features, including: city, town, village, factory, farm, house, office, port, harbour and shop
ncReferenceIndex.G.S1: Geography KS1 Skills and fieldwork: use world maps, atlases and globes to identify the United Kingdom and its countries, as well as the countries, continents and oceans studied at this key stage
ncReferenceIndex.G.S2: Geography KS1 Skills and fieldwork: use simple compass directions (North, South, East and West) and locational and directional language [for example, near and far; left and right], to describe the location of features and routes on a map
ncReferenceIndex.G.S3: Geography KS1 Skills and fieldwork: use aerial photographs and plan perspectives to recognise landmarks and basic human and physical features; devise a simple map; and use and construct basic symbols in a key
ncReferenceIndex.G.S4: Geography KS1 Skills and fieldwork: use simple fieldwork and observational skills to study the geography of their school and its grounds and the key human and physical features of its surrounding environment
ncReferenceIndex.A.1: Art and design KS1: to use a range of materials creatively to design and make products
ncReferenceIndex.A.2: Art and design KS1: to use drawing, painting and sculpture to develop and share their ideas, experiences and imagination
ncReferenceIndex.A.3: Art and design KS1: to develop a wide range of art and design techniques in using colour, pattern, texture, line, shape, form and space
ncReferenceIndex.A.4: Art and design KS1: about the work of a range of artists, craft makers and designers, describing the differences and similarities between different practices and disciplines, and making links to their own work
ncReferenceIndex.C.1: Computing KS1: understand what algorithms are; how they are implemented as programs on digital devices; and that programs execute by following precise and unambiguous instructions
ncReferenceIndex.C.2: Computing KS1: create and debug simple programs
ncReferenceIndex.C.3: Computing KS1: use logical reasoning to predict the behaviour of simple programs
ncReferenceIndex.C.4: Computing KS1: use technology purposefully to create, organise, store, manipulate and retrieve digital content
ncReferenceIndex.C.5: Computing KS1: recognise common uses of information technology beyond school
ncReferenceIndex.C.6: Computing KS1: use technology safely and respectfully, keeping personal information private; identify where to go for help and support when they have concerns about content or contact on the internet or other online technologies
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2NPV-1: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2NPV-1): recognise the place value of each digit in two-digit numbers, and compose and decompose two-digit numbers using standard and non-standard partitioning
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2NPV-2: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2NPV-2): reason about the location of any two-digit number in the linear number system, including identifying the previous and next multiple of 10
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2NF-1: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2NF-1): secure fluency in addition and subtraction facts within 10, through continued practice
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2AS-1: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2AS-1): add and subtract across 10
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2AS-2: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2AS-2): recognise the subtraction structure of 'difference' and answer questions of the form 'How many more...?'
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2AS-3: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2AS-3): add and subtract within 100 by applying related one-digit addition and subtraction facts: add and subtract only ones or only tens to/from a two-digit number
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2AS-4: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2AS-4): add and subtract within 100 by applying related one-digit addition and subtraction facts: add and subtract any 2 two-digit numbers
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2MD-1: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2MD-1): recognise repeated addition contexts, representing them with multiplication equations and calculating the product, within the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2MD-2: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2MD-2): relate grouping problems where the number of groups is unknown to multiplication equations with a missing factor, and to division equations (quotitive division)
ncReferenceIndex.RTP.2G-1: DfE ready-to-progress criteria, Year 2 (2G-1): use precise language to describe the properties of 2D and 3D shapes, and compare shapes by reasoning about similarities and differences in properties

subjects.name: English
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: English programmes of study, key stages 1 and 2 (DfE, 2013) - Year 2 programme of study, plus English Appendix 1 (Spelling) Year 2 statutory word list and rules, and English Appendix 2 (Vocabulary, grammar and punctuation) Year 2 requirements and terminology. Spoken language requirements are specified for Key Stage 1 as a whole.
subjects.overview: Five short playful sessions a week: a spelling rule taught, the rule applied together with common exception words, reading (word reading fluency and comprehension), handwriting or transcription, and grammar or writing composition. Year 2 is consolidation of phonics and the move into spelling patterns rather than new grapheme-phoneme correspondences: Autumn 1 reviews Phase 5, Autumn 2 bridges from phonics into spelling, and Spring and Summer work through the statutory Appendix 1 Year 2 spelling units. All 64 statutory Year 2 common exception words are introduced and then revisited. The Phonics Screening Check re-take falls in Summer 2 week 2.

weeks.unit: Phase 5 review: the many ways to write /ai/ and /ee/
weeks.phonicsPhase: Little Wandle Spelling Year 2 - Phase 5 review (Autumn 1, week 1)
gpcs: ai: a-e, ai, ay, a, eigh, ea, ey, aigh
ee: ee, ea, e, e-e, y, ie, ey

lessons.title: Sound Sort: all the ways to write /ai/
objectives: I can say the sound /ai/ when I see a-e, ai, ay, a, eigh or ea
I can sort words into the right /ai/ family
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Reading/word reading: read accurately by blending the sounds in words that contain the graphemes taught so far, especially recognising alternative sounds for graphemes
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Reads the split digraph a-e as two separate sounds, so cake becomes c-a-k-e
Thinks a grapheme can only ever make one sound, so reads 'break' with an /ee/ sound
teaches: /ai/ spelt a-e (cake, made)
/ai/ spelt ai (rain, train)
/ai/ spelt ay (day, play)
/ai/ spelt a (apron, acorn)
/ai/ spelt eigh (eight, weight)
/ai/ spelt ea (great, break, steak)

assessment.how: Post the word cards into six labelled 'letterboxes', one per spelling; she reads each word aloud before posting

lessons.bigRockReason: Year 2 spelling depends on knowing that one sound has several spellings - this is the mental map everything else hangs on

lessons.title: Best Bet: choosing a spelling for /ai/
objectives: I can pick the most likely way to spell /ai/ in a word
I know that ai almost never comes at the end of a word
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: learning new ways of spelling phonemes for which one or more spellings are already known, and learn some words with each spelling, including a few common homophones
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Uses ai at the end of a word (spelling play as 'plai')
Uses ay in the middle of a word (spelling rain as 'rayn')
teaches: ai is used in the middle of words; ay is used at the end
a-e is very common in the middle of words
great, break and steak are the only common words where /ai/ is spelt ea

assessment.how: Say a word, she holds up the ai / ay / a-e card she would bet on, then writes it on a whiteboard

lessons.title: The /ee/ Family and the Word Detective
objectives: I can read words where /ee/ is written ee, ea, e, e-e, y or ie
I can spot the /ee/ spelling inside a longer word
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Reading/word reading: read accurately by blending the sounds in words that contain the graphemes taught so far, especially recognising alternative sounds for graphemes
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Reads 'y' at the end of happy as /igh/ rather than /ee/
Cannot hold a two-syllable word together, reading 'monkey' as two unconnected chunks
teaches: /ee/ spelt ee (sheep)
/ee/ spelt ea (dream)
/ee/ spelt e (he, she, me)
/ee/ spelt e-e (these)
/ee/ spelt y at the end of words (happy, sunny)
/ee/ spelt ie (chief, field)

assessment.how: Word-detective hunt through a favourite book: she finds and reads five /ee/ words and names the spelling

lessons.title: Handwriting: letters that sit, hang and reach
objectives: I can write my letters the right size next to each other
I can make my tall letters tall and my hanging letters hang
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/handwriting: form lower-case letters of the correct size relative to one another
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Makes every letter the same height so 'h' and 'n' look identical
Leaves gaps so large that words look like separate lines of writing
teaches: Letters with ascenders: b d f h k l t
Letters with descenders: g j p q y
The finger space is about the width of one letter, not a whole hand

assessment.how: She writes 'the happy dog' and checks it against a three-line guide; you praise the two best-sized letters

lessons.title: Talk and Write: my summer in three sentences
objectives: I can say my sentence out loud before I write it
I can put a capital letter and a full stop on every sentence
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/composition: consider what they are going to write before beginning by planning or saying out loud what they are going to write about
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Writes one very long sentence joined by 'and' all the way through
Uses a capital letter only at the very start of the whole piece
teaches: Say it, then write it, then read it back
Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop

assessment.how: She reads her three sentences aloud to a toy and you both count the full stops

knowledgeComponents.statement: /ai/ can be written a-e, ai, ay, a, eigh or ea
ai is used in the middle of a word
ay is used at the end of a word
great, break and steak are the only common words where /ai/ is spelt ea
/ee/ can be written ee, ea, e, e-e, y or ie
y at the end of a word usually says /ee/, as in happy
door is spelled d-o-o-r
floor is spelled f-l-o-o-r
poor is spelled p-o-o-r
people is spelled p-e-o-p-l-e
Letters with ascenders (b d f h k l t) are tall; letters with descenders (g j p q y) hang below the line
Every sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop

weeks.unit: Phase 5 review: /igh/ and /oa/, and the /igh/ sound spelt -y
weeks.phonicsPhase: Little Wandle Spelling Year 2 - Phase 5 review (Autumn 1, week 2)
gpcs: igh: igh, i-e, i, y, ie
oa: oa, ow, o, o-e, oe, ou

lessons.title: Sound Sort: the many ways to write /igh/
objectives: I can read words where /igh/ is written igh, i-e, i, y or ie
I can sort /igh/ words into families
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Reading/word reading: read accurately by blending the sounds in words that contain the graphemes taught so far, especially recognising alternative sounds for graphemes
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Reads 'find' with a short /i/ because the i is not followed by a magic e
Reads final y as /ee/ in every word, so 'fly' becomes 'flee'
teaches: /igh/ spelt igh (light, night)
/igh/ spelt i-e (bike, time)
/igh/ spelt i (find, kind, mind, behind, child, wild)
/igh/ spelt y (fly, cry)
/igh/ spelt ie (pie, tie)

assessment.how: Snap with word cards: she snaps when two cards share the same /igh/ spelling

lessons.title: Spelling rule: /igh/ at the end of a word is written y
objectives: I know that /igh/ at the end of a word is nearly always written y
I can spell cry, fly, dry, try, reply and July
lessons.ncRef: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /igh/ sound spelt -y at the end of words - this is by far the most common spelling for this sound at the end of words (cry, fly, dry, try, reply, July)
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Spells fly as 'fligh' because igh is the spelling she knows best
Adds a silent e, spelling try as 'trie'
teaches: The /igh/ sound spelt -y at the end of words: cry, fly, dry, try, reply, July
This is by far the most common spelling for this sound at the end of words

assessment.how: Sky-write then whiteboard-write six words to beat a one-minute sand timer; she marks her own with a green pen

lessons.bigRockReason: First explicit statutory Year 2 Appendix 1 spelling rule - it establishes that position in the word decides the spelling

lessons.title: Sound Sort: the many ways to write /oa/
objectives: I can read words where /oa/ is written oa, ow, o, o-e or oe
I can read /oa/ words with two syllables
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Reading/word reading: read accurately by blending the sounds in words that contain the graphemes taught so far, especially recognising alternative sounds for graphemes

objectives: I can choose a word or phrase I love from a book
I can say why I like it
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Reading/comprehension: discussing their favourite words and phrases
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.

Discussing and clarifying the meanings of words, linking new meanings to known vocabulary

lessons.title: Grammar: the progressive form - what is happening right now
objectives: I can say what is happening at this very moment
I can use is and was with an -ing verb
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/vocabulary, grammar and punctuation: learn how to use the present and past tenses correctly and consistently including the progressive form
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Drops the helper verb: 'she drumming'

teaches: Use of the progressive form of verbs in the present and past tense to mark actions in progress, for example she is drumming, he was shouting

assessment.how: Freeze-frame game: she mimes an action and you both narrate 'She is hopping' then 'She was hopping'

knowledgeComponents.statement: Add -ing to most verbs with no change to the root word
If a one-syllable word ends in one consonant after one short vowel, double the consonant before -ing
The letter x is never doubled
The three-question check: one syllable? short vowel? one consonant at the end?
plant is spelled p-l-a-n-t
path is spelled p-a-t-h
bath is spelled b-a-t-h
The root word is the word left when the suffix is taken off
The present progressive uses is or are plus an -ing verb: she is drumming
The past progressive uses was or were plus an -ing verb: he was shouting
A suffix is an ending added to a root word
running is spelled r-u-n-n-i-n-g

weeks.phonicsPhase: Little Wandle Spelling Year 2 - Bridge to spelling (Autumn 2, week 6)

lessons.title: Adding -ed: three different sounds, one spelling
objectives: I know that -ed can sound like /d/, /t/ or /id/

lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: apply spelling rules and guidance, as listed in English Appendix 1
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Spells jumped as 'jumpt' because of the /t/ sound
Adds an extra syllable: 'jump-ed'
teaches: Adding -ed to verbs: played /d/, jumped /t/, wanted /id/
The sound changes but the spelling is always -ed

assessment.how: Three-basket sort: /d/, /t/ and /id/ - she says each word and posts it in the right basket

lessons.bigRockReason: Hearing three sounds but writing one spelling is a genuine conceptual leap and it prevents a very common error

lessons.title: Doubling before -ed
objectives: I can use the three-question check before I add -ed
I can spell hopped, patted, dropped and hummed
lessons.ncRef: English Appendix 1 (Y2): adding -ing, -ed, -er, -est and -y to words of one syllable ending in a single consonant letter after a single vowel letter - the last consonant letter of the root word is doubled to keep the short vowel sound; exception: the letter x is never doubled (patting, patted, humming, hummed, dropping, dropped, sadder, saddest, fatter, fattest, runner, runny)
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Doubles when the vowel is long: 'hoped' becomes 'hopped' and changes the meaning

teaches: patted, hummed, dropped, hopped, fitted
hoped and hopped are different words: the double letter keeps the vowel short

assessment.how: Hope or hop? She reads a sentence and decides which spelling belongs there

lessons.title: Common exception words: hour, move, prove, improve
objectives: I can read and spell hour, move, prove and improve
I can point to the surprising letters
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: learning to spell common exception words
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Reads hour with a sounded h
Spells move as 'moov'
teaches: hour, move, prove, improve
The h in hour is silent; the ove in move, prove and improve says /oov/

assessment.how: Silent-letter detective: she circles the letter that makes no sound in each word

lessons.title: Reading: recurring language in stories and poems
objectives: I can spot a phrase that keeps coming back
I can join in with it
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Reading/comprehension: recognising simple recurring literary language in stories and poetry
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Notices the repetition but does not expect it to come again
Thinks 'Once upon a time' is the only story language there is
teaches: Recognising simple recurring literary language in stories and poetry
Traditional tales use phrases like 'Once upon a time', 'long, long ago' and 'they all lived happily ever after'

assessment.how: Join-in reading: she chants the refrain every time it comes round, louder each time

lessons.title: Writing: retelling a traditional tale
objectives: I can retell a story I know well in my own words
I can use storyteller language

misconceptions: Retells only the famous scene and leaves out the beginning
Uses the same joining word for every sentence
teaches: Becoming increasingly familiar with and retelling a wider range of stories, fairy stories and traditional tales

knowledgeComponents.statement: The suffix -ed can sound like /d/, /t/ or /id/ but is always spelt e-d
If a one-syllable word ends in one consonant after one short vowel, double the consonant before -ed
hoped and hopped are different words - the double letter keeps the vowel short
hour is spelled h-o-u-r and the h is silent
move is spelled m-o-v-e
prove is spelled p-r-o-v-e
improve is spelled i-m-p-r-o-v-e
A refrain is a phrase that comes back again and again in a story or poem
Traditional tales often begin 'Once upon a time' and end 'happily ever after'
Retelling means telling a known story in your own words, keeping the order
jumped is spelled j-u-m-p-e-d even though it sounds like /jumpt/
wanted is spelled w-a-n-t-e-d and the -ed adds an extra beat

weeks.unit: Bridge to spelling: swapping y for i, and writing for Christmas
weeks.phonicsPhase: Little Wandle Spelling Year 2 - Bridge to spelling (Autumn 2, week 7)
gpcs: y changed to i before -ed, -er and -est

lessons.title: Swap the y for an i - but not before -ing
objectives: I can change y to i before -ed, -er and -est
I know to keep the y before -ing
lessons.ncRef: English Appendix 1 (Y2): adding -ed, -ing, -er and -est to a root word ending in -y with a consonant before it - the y is changed to i before -ed, -er and -est are added, but not before -ing as this would result in ii (copied, copier, happier, happiest, cried, replied, copying, crying, replying)
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Swaps the y before -ing, producing 'criing'
Applies the rule to words with a vowel before the y, so 'played' becomes 'plaied'
teaches: Adding -ed, -er and -est to a root word ending in -y with a consonant before it: the y is changed to i (copied, copier, happier, happiest, cried, replied)
The y is not changed before -ing, as this would result in ii (copying, crying, replying)

assessment.how: Swap-shop: she physically swaps a y tile for an i tile, and refuses the swap when -ing comes along

lessons.bigRockReason: This is the rule Year 2 children get wrong most often, and the 'not before -ing' exception is what makes it stick

lessons.title: Apply it: dictation with this term's rules
objectives: I can write two sentences from memory
I can use the spelling rules I have learnt this term
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: write from memory simple sentences dictated by the teacher that include words using the GPCs, common exception words and punctuation taught so far
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Writes fast and does not check the ending rules
Corrects only spellings, not punctuation
teaches: Writing from memory simple sentences dictated by the teacher including words using the GPCs, common exception words and punctuation taught so far

assessment.how: Dictation then rule-hunt: she circles every word in her sentence that used a rule and names the rule

lessons.title: Common exception words: Christmas, money, half
objectives: I can read and spell Christmas, money and half
I can use a capital letter for Christmas
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: learning to spell common exception words
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Writes christmas with a small c
Spells half as 'harf' or 'haf'
teaches: Christmas, money, half
Christmas is a proper noun and always takes a capital letter; the l in half is silent

assessment.how: Christmas card writing with the three words used correctly at least once

lessons.title: Poetry: writing a winter poem
objectives: I can write a poem about winter
I can choose words that sound good together
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/composition: develop positive attitudes towards and stamina for writing by writing poetry
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Believes a poem must rhyme and forces bad rhymes
Writes prose in short lines and calls it a poem
teaches: Writing poetry
A poem can use the senses instead of rhyme: what I see, hear, smell, feel

assessment.how: She performs the poem by candlelight or fairy lights to whoever is around

lessons.title: Writing: a Christmas recount to keep
objectives: I can write about something that really happened, with my sentences in order
I can read it back and fix anything that does not make sense
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/composition: develop positive attitudes towards and stamina for writing by writing about real events
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Adds detail as it occurs to her rather than in order
Reads back what she meant to write rather than what is on the page
teaches: Re-reading to check that their writing makes sense and that verbs to indicate time are used correctly and consistently
Proof-reading to check for errors in spelling, grammar and punctuation

assessment.how: The finished piece goes into a keep-forever folder; she reads it aloud on Christmas Day

knowledgeComponents.statement: Change y to i before -ed, -er and -est when there is a consonant before the y
Keep the y before -ing, because ii is not allowed
cried is spelled c-r-i-e-d and crying is spelled c-r-y-i-n-g
happier is spelled h-a-p-p-i-e-r and happiest is spelled h-a-p-p-i-e-s-t
Christmas is spelled C-h-r-i-s-t-m-a-s and always takes a capital letter
money is spelled m-o-n-e-y
half is spelled h-a-l-f and the l is silent
A proper noun is the name of a particular person, place or day and takes a capital letter
A poem does not have to rhyme
Proofreading means checking what is actually on the page, not what you meant to write
Reading your writing aloud is the fastest way to hear a sentence that does not make sense
copies is spelled c-o-p-i-e-s

weeks.unit: Unit 1a: the /n/ sound spelt kn and gn at the beginning of words

lessons.title: Silent letters at the start: kn and gn
objectives: I can read words that start with kn or gn
I can spell knock, know, knee, gnat and gnaw
lessons.ncRef: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /n/ sound spelt kn and (less often) gn at the beginning of words - the 'k' and 'g' at the beginning of these words was sounded hundreds of years ago (knock, know, knee, gnat, gnaw)
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Sounds the k, reading knee as 'k-nee'
Leaves the k out when spelling, writing 'nock' for knock
teaches: The /n/ sound spelt kn and (less often) gn at the beginning of words: knock, know, knee, gnat, gnaw
The k and g at the beginning of these words was sounded hundreds of years ago

assessment.how: Knock-knock game: every knock-knock joke answer must contain a kn or gn word she writes down

lessons.bigRockReason: The first true spelling unit of the year, and the idea that spelling carries history is genuinely memorable at six

lessons.title: Building the kn word family
objectives: I can write a list of kn words
I can use one of them in a sentence
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: apply spelling rules and guidance, as listed in English Appendix 1
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Assumes every /n/ word might start with kn and over-applies the pattern
Writes the word correctly in a list but not inside a sentence
teaches: kn words: knock, know, knee, knife, knot, knight, knew, knit, knuckle
gn words: gnat, gnaw, gnome, gnash

assessment.how: Knee-tap spelling: she taps her knee once per letter while spelling each word aloud

lessons.title: Common exception words: could, should, would
objectives: I can read and spell could, should and would
I can see they all share the same tricky bit
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: learning to spell common exception words
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Spells could as 'cud' or 'cood'
Learns could but treats should and would as unrelated
teaches: could, should, would
All three end with the same letters -ould, with a silent l

assessment.how: O-U-L-D chant: she chants the four letters then adds c, sh or w on the front

lessons.title: Reading: asking my own questions about a book
objectives: I can ask a good question about what I am reading
I can ask a question the book does not answer
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Reading/comprehension: answering and asking questions
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Asks questions she already knows the answer to
Waits to be asked rather than asking
teaches: Answering and asking questions
Asking relevant questions to extend their understanding and knowledge

assessment.how: Question swap: she asks you three questions about the book and you ask her three back

lessons.title: Grammar: subordination with because
objectives: I can add a because part to my sentence
I can explain why something happened
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/vocabulary, grammar and punctuation: learn how to use subordination (using when, if, that, or because) and co-ordination (using or, and, or but)
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Starts a sentence with 'Because' and leaves it unfinished
Uses 'because' where 'so' is needed, reversing cause and effect
teaches: Subordination (using when, if, that, because)
The because part gives the reason and cannot stand alone as a sentence

assessment.how: Because-chain: you say a sentence, she adds a because, you add a because to that

knowledgeComponents.statement: The /n/ sound is spelt kn and less often gn at the beginning of some words
knock, know, knee, knife, knot, knight and knit begin with a silent k
gnat, gnaw and gnome begin with a silent g
The k and g in these words were really sounded hundreds of years ago
could is spelled c-o-u-l-d
should is spelled s-h-o-u-l-d
would is spelled w-o-u-l-d
could, should and would all end -ould
because introduces a reason and cannot stand alone as a sentence
A good question about a book is one you do not already know the answer to
night and knight are homophones
A subordinating conjunction such as because, when, if or that adds a part that depends on the main sentence

weeks.unit: Unit 1b: the /r/ sound spelt wr at the beginning of words

lessons.title: Silent w: write, written, wrote, wrong, wrap
objectives: I can read words that start with wr
I can spell write, wrote, wrong and wrap
lessons.ncRef: English Appendix 1 (Y2): the /r/ sound spelt wr at the beginning of words - this spelling probably also reflects an old pronunciation (write, written, wrote, wrong, wrap)
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Leaves out the w when spelling, writing 'rite' for write
Confuses write and right
teaches: The /r/ sound spelt wr at the beginning of words: write, written, wrote, wrong, wrap
This spelling probably also reflects an old pronunciation

assessment.how: Wriggly writing: she writes each wr word with a wiggly line under the silent w

lessons.title: Homophones: knight and night, write and right
objectives: I can tell two words apart when they sound the same
I can choose the right one for the meaning
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: distinguishing between homophones and near-homophones

Believes homophones are simply two spellings of the same word

night/knight, write/right, sea/see, here/hear

lessons.title: Common exception words: who and whole
objectives: I can read and spell who and whole
I can hear that whole and hole sound the same

Uses hole when whole is meant

whole and hole are homophones; whole means all of something

objectives: I can join into tall letters neatly
I can keep my tall letters tall

lessons.title: Writing: a story about someone else
objectives: I can write a story about a character who is not me
I can say what my character wants
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/composition: develop positive attitudes towards and stamina for writing by writing narratives about personal experiences and those of others (real and fictional)
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.

Gives the character no problem, so nothing happens
teaches: Writing narratives about personal experiences and those of others (real and fictional)
Writing down ideas and/or key words, including new vocabulary

knowledgeComponents.statement: The /r/ sound is spelt wr at the beginning of some words
write, written, wrote, wrong and wrap begin with a silent w
Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and different meanings
night is the dark time; a knight wears armour
write means to put words on paper; right means correct or the opposite of left
who is spelled w-h-o
whole is spelled w-h-o-l-e and means all of something
whole and hole are homophones
Ascenders stay full height even when the letter is joined
A story character needs to want something, or nothing happens
Planning key words before writing makes the writing easier
wrap and rap are homophones

weeks.unit: Unit 2a: dropping the e before -ed, -ing, -er, -est and -y
gpcs: dropping the silent e before a vowel suffix

lessons.title: Drop the e: hike, hiking, hiked, hiker
objectives: I can drop the e before I add -ing, -ed, -er, -est or -y
I can spell hiking, hiked, nicer, nicest and shiny

lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Keeps the e, writing 'hikeing' and 'niceer'
Drops the e before a consonant suffix, writing 'nicly' for nicely
teaches: The -e at the end of the root word is dropped before -ing, -ed, -er, -est, -y or any other suffix beginning with a vowel letter
hiking, hiked, hiker, nicer, nicest, shiny
Exception: being

lessons.title: Drop it or keep it? Sorting the suffixes

lessons.ncRef: English Appendix 1 (Y2): adding the endings -ing, -ed, -er, -est and -y to words ending in -e with a consonant before it - the -e at the end of the root word is dropped before -ing, -ed, -er, -est, -y or any other suffix beginning with a vowel letter is added; exception: being (hiking, hiked, hiker, nicer, nicest, shiny)
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.

lessons.title: Common exception words: class, grass, pass, again, two

I can use them in a sentence I make up
lessons.ncRef: English Y2 Writing/transcription: learning to spell common exception words
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.

lessons.title: Reading: two-syllable and three-syllable words
objectives: I can break a long word into chunks and read it
I can read words of two or more syllables

lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.

lessons.title: Grammar: subordination with when, if and that

knowledgeComponents.statement: c says /s/ before e, i and y

race, ice, cell, city, fancy, circle and pencil all use soft c

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, key stages 1 and 2 (DfE, 2013) - Year 2 programme of study; sequenced with reference to the White Rose Maths Year 2 scheme of learning and mapped against the DfE ready-to-progress criteria for Year 2 from Mathematics guidance: key stages 1 and 2 (DfE, 2020).
subjects.overview: Four short playful sessions a week: teach with concrete objects, practise pictorially through a game, reason and solve problems, and a short daily number-fact session. The year runs place value to 100, addition and subtraction, shape, money, multiplication and division including the 2, 5 and 10 times tables, statistics, fractions, length and height, mass, capacity and temperature, time, and position and direction. Every one of the ten Year 2 ready-to-progress criteria is explicitly carried by named weeks.

subjects.name: Science
subjects.ncReference: National curriculum in England: science programmes of study, key stages 1 and 2 (DfE, 2013) - Key Stage 1 working scientifically and the Year 2 programme of study: Living things and their habitats; Plants; Animals, including humans; Uses of everyday materials.
subjects.overview: Two short, almost entirely practical sessions a week. Living things and their habitats is split across Autumn 1 and Summer 2 so the fieldwork happens in warm weather; Uses of everyday materials sits indoors in Autumn 2; Animals including humans runs through the spring; and Plants sits in Summer 1 so a three-week growing investigation has time to happen. Working scientifically is woven through every week rather than taught separately, and the five types of enquiry are named explicitly.

lessons.title: A timeline of my Discover year
objectives: I can put everything I have studied in order
I can say what I found most interesting
lessons.ncRef: History KS1: pupils should develop an awareness of the past, using common words and phrases relating to the passing of time; know where the people and events they study fit within a chronological framework and identify similarities and differences between ways of life in different periods; use a wide vocabulary of everyday historical terms
lessons.sessionNote: Short, playful and untimed - 10 to 20 minutes, stop when she has had enough. Year 2 can carry a little more reading and writing than Year 1, but she is still six: most of the thinking happens out loud, with objects in her hands, and instructions are spoken, not read.
misconceptions: Orders topics by when she studied them rather than when they happened
Cannot connect topics from different half terms
teaches: Know where the people and events they study fit within a chronological framework

assessment.how: A big wall timeline covering Elizabeth I, the first flight, Elizabeth II and today

knowledgeComponents.statement: Elizabeth I reigned in the 1500s and 1600s
The first aeroplane flight was in 1903
Elizabeth II reigned from 1952 to 2022
A chronological framework helps you see how events fit together in time
Topics studied in a different order still happened in a fixed order
Reviewing a year of learning shows connections you did not notice at the time
History, geography, art and computing all connect to each other
Putting topics on one timeline shows how they relate to each other in time

knowledgeComponents.statement: Explaining your work to someone else shows what you really understood
The seven continents and five oceans are worth knowing by heart
Maps, timelines, artworks and programs are all ways of showing what you know
Curiosity about what comes next is the point of learning
An exhibition needs labels so visitors know what they are looking at
Being proud of your work is different from it being perfect
History, geography, art and computing each ask different kinds of question
Showing your work to an audience is how you find out what you can explain
